message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"10.6","text":"Take courage, then, and approach God—you who were made at the beginning to rule and exercise lordship over everything, who have his image in the body and likewise possess in the mind the likeness of will. Since, then, by doing things resembling irrational animals you lost from your soul the soul of a human being, you became like pigs and became what demons ask for. If, then, you accept God’s law, you become human beings. For it is not possible to say to irrational animals, “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” and the rest. Therefore, do not begrudge yourselves entering your original nobility when you are called back to it. For it is possible. If you become like God through good deeds, then, having been reckoned his sons because of the likeness, you will be able to be restored as masters of everything.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπὶ τῷ πάντων ἄρχειν καὶ κυριεύειν γεγενημένοι","chosen":"made at the beginning to rule and exercise lordship over everything","rationale":"Treats τὴν ἀρχήν temporally and preserves the distinction between ἄρχειν and κυριεύειν."},{"source_quote":"ἐν τῷ νῷ τῆς γνώμης τὴν ὁμοιότητα","chosen":"possess in the mind the likeness of will","rationale":"γνώμη can denote will, disposition, purpose, or judgment. “Will” fits the contrast between bodily image and mental or volitional likeness without adding an explicit possessive absent from the phrase."},{"source_quote":"δαιμόνων αἰτήματα ἐγένεσθε","chosen":"became what demons ask for","rationale":"Literally, “became requests of demons.” The contextual rendering treats αἰτήματα as the objects requested, likely invoking demons’ request concerning pigs; “became demons’ demands” is another possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"μὴ φθονέσητε ἑαυτοῖς","chosen":"do not begrudge yourselves","rationale":"Preserves the reflexive force and the sense of withholding a good from oneself."},{"source_quote":"πάντων δεσπόται ἀποκαταστῆναι","chosen":"be restored as masters of everything","rationale":"Takes πάντων with δεσπόται and retains the restoration motif established earlier in the section."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἐκ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴν ἀπωλέσατε","issue":"The repetition of ψυχή produces the semantically unusual statement “you lost from your soul the soul of a human being.” The supplied reading is translatable and has been preserved rather than silently changed, though rhetorical paradox or textual disturbance remains possible.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"10.7","text":"Begin, then, to strip off the harmful fears of empty idols, so that you may escape unjust slavery. For they have become your masters, though they are useless to you even as servants. I mean the material of the lifeless statues, which are of no use even in serving you. For it neither hears nor sees nor perceives; indeed, it cannot even move. Or does any of you wish to see as it sees, to hear as it hears, and to perceive and move? But far be it to insult any human being at all with such an insult, one who carries God’s image around, even if he has lost the likeness.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀποδύεσθαι τῶν κενῶν εἰδώλων τοὺς ἐπιβλαβεῖς φόβους","chosen":"strip off the harmful fears of empty idols","rationale":"Preserves the clothing metaphor in ἀποδύεσθαι and allows the genitive to identify the idols that occasion or receive the fears."},{"source_quote":"οἳ καὶ εἰς δούλους ὑμῖν ἄχρηστοι τυγχάνουσιν","chosen":"though they are useless to you even as servants","rationale":"The idols are contrasted with the mastery wrongly granted to them: they would be useless even in the subordinate role of servants."},{"source_quote":"λέγω δὲ περὶ ὕλης","chosen":"I mean the material","rationale":"The singular pronouns in the following sentence naturally refer to ὕλη, the statue’s inert material, rather than to the preceding plural statues."},{"source_quote":"οὕτως ὁρᾶν ὡς ὁρᾷ καὶ ἀκούειν ὡς ἀκούει","chosen":"to see as it sees, to hear as it hears","rationale":"Retains the deliberately absurd comparison with the sight and hearing of insensible material."},{"source_quote":"ἀπείη τοιαύτῃ λοιδορίᾳ λοιδορεῖν πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν ἄνθρωπον","chosen":"far be it to insult any human being at all with such an insult","rationale":"Preserves the emphatic repudiation, the repetition of the λοιδορία word group, and the comprehensive force of πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"10.8","text":"Restore, at any rate, your gods—those of gold and silver, or those made from any other material—to their original nature: to bowls, I mean, and basins and all the other things that can be useful in serving you. And these good things, given to you from the beginning, will be able to be restored to you. But perhaps you will say, “The laws of those in authority do not permit us to do this.” Good! It is laws, and not the nonexistent power of the vain objects of worship themselves. How, then, have you regarded as gods those who are defended by human laws, guarded by dogs, and secured by bars? And this is so if they are of gold, silver, or bronze; for the stone or earthenware ones are protected by their lack of value, because no human being desires to steal a stone or earthenware god. Thus your gods made from more costly material are exposed to great danger. How, then, are they even gods when they are stolen, melted down, weighed, and hammered?","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εἰς τὴν πρώτην αὐτῶν φύσιν ἀποκαταστήσατε","chosen":"restore ... to their original nature","rationale":"The statues’ materials are to be returned to their prior, useful forms, preserving both φύσις and the restoration language."},{"source_quote":"εἴς τε φιάλας λέγω καὶ λεκάνας","chosen":"to bowls, I mean, and basins","rationale":"φιάλη denotes a broad or shallow bowl, while λεκάνη denotes a basin; λέγω marks the author’s clarification."},{"source_quote":"οἱ τῶν ἐφεστώτων νόμοι","chosen":"the laws of those in authority","rationale":"ἐφεστῶτες are those standing over others, hence rulers or authorities; the less specific rendering preserves the source’s formulation."},{"source_quote":"καλῶς ὅτι Νόμοι, καὶ οὐκ αὐτῶν τῶν εἰκαίων σεβασμάτων ἡ μὴ οὖσα δύναμις","chosen":"Good! It is laws, and not the nonexistent power of the vain objects of worship themselves","rationale":"The compressed retort contrasts the actual restraint of civil laws with the nonexistent power of the objects being revered. εἰκαῖος can mean vain, idle, or groundless."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ ἀνθρωπίνων νόμων ἐκδικουμένους","chosen":"defended by human laws","rationale":"ἐκδικέω in the passive can mean avenged, vindicated, or protected. “Defended” best fits laws preventing the statues’ destruction or removal."},{"source_quote":"τὰ γὰρ λίθινα ἢ ὀστράκινα","chosen":"the stone or earthenware ones","rationale":"ὀστράκινος denotes material made from fired clay or earthenware, not merely an object shaped like a shell."},{"source_quote":"κλεπτόμενοι, χωνευόμενοι, σταθμιζόμενοι, σφυρούμενοι","chosen":"stolen, melted down, weighed, and hammered","rationale":"Preserves all four passive participles and the sequence of actions to which valuable metal images are subjected."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"10.9","text":"Ah, the minds of wretched human beings, afraid of things deader than corpses! For I cannot even call things that have never lived dead—unless, that is, they are tombs of ancient people. Sometimes someone arriving in unfamiliar places does not know whether the temples he sees are memorials of dead men or of the so-called gods. But after asking and hearing that they belong to gods, he worships, without being ashamed that, if he had not learned by inquiry, he would have passed one by as a dead man’s monument because of the exact resemblance. Still, I need not furnish extensive proof against superstition of this kind. For anyone willing to understand can easily grasp that it is nothing—unless someone does not see. Nevertheless, at least now hear that it does not hear, and understand that it does not understand. For the hands of a man who died “made it.” And if the one who made it came to his end, how will what came into being through him not be dissolved? Why, then, do you worship a mortal’s work, when it is entirely without sensation and people who possess reason do not even worship animals or pay court to the elements made by God—I mean heaven, sun, moon, stars, earth, sea, and everything in them—but correctly judge that they should not worship the things made by him, but should revere God, the creator and provider of these things? For these things themselves also rejoice in this: that no one has attached to them the honor belonging to the one who made them.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"νεκρῶν νεκρότερα","chosen":"deader than corpses","rationale":"The comparative image is retained; νεκροί here naturally denotes dead persons or corpses rather than abstractly “the dead.”"},{"source_quote":"εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν","chosen":"unless, that is, they are tombs of ancient people","rationale":"Treats the stacked exceptive wording εἰ μὴ ἐκτός as emphatic. The alternative “unless perhaps” gives a similar contextual sense."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὸ ἴσον τῆς ὁμοιότητος","chosen":"because of the exact resemblance","rationale":"Literally referring to the equality of the likeness, the phrase stresses that a temple and a tomb are indistinguishable in appearance."},{"source_quote":"πρὸς τὴν τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας πολλὴν παρέχειν ἀπόδειξιν","chosen":"furnish extensive proof against superstition of this kind","rationale":"πρός is taken in an argumentative sense; “concerning superstition of this kind” is also grammatically possible."},{"source_quote":"πλὴν κἂν νῦν ἄκουσον","chosen":"Nevertheless, at least now hear","rationale":"In this exhortation κἄν has the concessive-minimal force “at least,” rather than introducing a full conditional clause."},{"source_quote":"χεῖρες γὰρ αὐτὸ θανόντος ἀνθρώπου „ἐποίησαν“","chosen":"the hands of a man who died “made it”","rationale":"Preserves the source’s quotation marking around ἐποίησαν and the singular object αὐτό."},{"source_quote":"ὁπότε οἱ λογισμοὺς ἔχοντες","chosen":"when ... people who possess reason","rationale":"The clause is attached to the preceding rhetorical question as a contrasting circumstance. It could instead be presented as a loosely independent “seeing that” or “whereas” sentence; the edition’s punctuation does not require emendation."},{"source_quote":"οὐδὲ στοιχεῖα τὰ ὑπὸ θεοῦ γεγενημένα κολακεύουσιν","chosen":"do not ... pay court to the elements made by God","rationale":"στοιχεῖα denotes cosmic elements or constituent parts of the world, while κολακεύω literally evokes flattering or courting them."},{"source_quote":"τὸν τούτων δημιουργὸν καὶ πάροχον σέβειν θεόν","chosen":"revere God, the creator and provider of these things","rationale":"πάροχος can denote a provider, supplier, or giver. “Provider” preserves its distinction from δημιουργός, “creator.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν","issue":"The combination εἰ μὴ ἐκτός is unusually redundant as an exceptive expression. A defensible emphatic reading is available, so the supplied text is retained without conjectural correction.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"10.10","text":"For glory worthy of honor belongs to him alone, the only unoriginated one, since everything else has come into being. Just as being God, then, belongs uniquely to the unoriginated one, so anything at all that has come into being is not truly God. Above all, therefore, you must understand the malicious scheme of the serpent that is deceiving you from within. It cleverly deceives you with the promise of better reasoning, crawling from your brain into your spinal marrow and regarding your being deceived as a great gain.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἡ ἔντιμος δόξα","chosen":"glory worthy of honor","rationale":"ἔντιμος describes something honored, esteemed, or worthy of honor. The rendering avoids turning the adjective and noun into two separate source claims."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ μόνου ἀγενήτου","chosen":"the only unoriginated one","rationale":"ἀγένητος is contrasted here with γενητός and γενόμενον, so “unoriginated” preserves the coming-into-being contrast more precisely than “unbegotten.”"},{"source_quote":"πᾶν ὁτιοῦν γενόμενον θεὸς τῷ ὄντι οὐκ ἔστιν","chosen":"anything at all that has come into being is not truly God","rationale":"πᾶν ὁτιοῦν is emphatically comprehensive, while τῷ ὄντι means “in reality” or “truly.”"},{"source_quote":"τὴν τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἀπατῶντος ὄφεως κακοῦργον ἐπίνοιαν","chosen":"the malicious scheme of the serpent that is deceiving you from within","rationale":"ἐν ὑμῖν may describe either the serpent’s location or the sphere of its deception. “From within” preserves both possibilities without identifying the serpent with a specific anatomical structure."},{"source_quote":"φρονίμως ὑμᾶς ἀπατᾷ ὑποσχέσει κρείττονος λογισμοῦ","chosen":"cleverly deceives you with the promise of better reasoning","rationale":"φρονίμως is ironic here and means intelligently or shrewdly; λογισμός may mean reasoning, calculation, or thought."},{"source_quote":"ἕρπων ὑμῶν ἐκ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου εἰς τὸν νωτιαῖον μυελὸν","chosen":"crawling from your brain into your spinal marrow","rationale":"Retains the anatomical image and the serpent’s downward movement from the brain into the spinal cord or marrow."},{"source_quote":"μέγα κέρδος ἡγούμενος τὴν ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην","chosen":"regarding your being deceived as a great gain","rationale":"ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην could formally mean “your deception,” including deception practiced by you, but the repeated claim that the serpent deceives the audience favors the objective sense, their being deceived."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
